dialogue.speaker: Desmond Park
dialogue.content:
*His cart appears at the corridor's far end — not the same floor, but close enough. He's restocking a supply cabinet near the 12th-floor alcove, quiet and unhurried, and when he rounds the corner he clocks Jordan still rooted in front of the CLOSED photograph. He doesn't announce himself this time. Just works. Thirty seconds pass.*

Most people read the rejection letter first. Proof they tried, proof someone said no — feels like the dramatic center. You went straight to the photograph.

*He doesn't look up from the cabinet. His voice carries without being raised — the practiced volume of someone used to speaking in spaces where sound travels.*

That mine operated for eleven years at a loss before it closed. Marlene bought the mineral rights off a bankruptcy estate for forty dollars and a handshake. The gold was already in the quartz. She just needed a different question — not 'is there gold' but 'does anyone else know how to see it yet.'

*Now he does look at Jordan. Brief, direct.*

You've got about ninety seconds before the group notices you're missing. They will notice. Your call whether that matters.

*He closes the cabinet, wheels the cart forward, unhurried.*

dialogue.speaker: User
dialogue.content: Ask Desmond directly: does Marlene actually watch this corridor, or is that building mythology

dialogue.speaker: Desmond Park
dialogue.content:
*He stops the cart. Doesn't turn around immediately — takes a half-second that feels considered rather than evasive, then looks back over his shoulder.*

Both.

*He lets that land, then pulls the cart to the corridor wall so it's clear of the walkway — a small, deliberate act of staying.*

The cameras are real. Whether she's watching *right now* — that's the mythology part. But here's the distinction that matters: she reviews. Not live, not obsessively. She looks at the footage when someone interests her. Which means the question isn't whether you're being watched today.

*He faces Jordan fully now, arms loose at his sides.*

The question is whether you do anything today worth reviewing later.

*A beat. Down the corridor, muffled voices — the group is wrapping up, movement sounds, Felix's laugh carrying cleanly through the recycled air.*

You came in on a Thursday application that got a Monday call. That already interested someone. The corridor footage from this morning will show you stopped at the photograph for four minutes while three other candidates logged under ninety seconds combined.

*He picks up the cart handle.*

Go catch your group. And when Dana Voss schedules your first individual check-in — she will, by Wednesday — don't pitch what you prepared. Pitch what you just figured out standing here.

dialogue.speaker: Desmond Park

*He's already moving — cart rolling soft against polished concrete, heading toward the service corridor. He doesn't watch Jordan go. Doesn't need to.*

*The group is thirty feet ahead, clustered near the framed napkin plan — Felix holding court, pointing at the handwriting with the easy authority of someone who's already decided what the correct reading is. The two other interns, Marcus and Celia, are nodding at the right intervals. The kind of nodding that is really just waiting.*

*Jordan slots in beside them naturally enough. Felix glances over — that calibrated smile, half a degree warmer than it needs to be.*

Felix Arrandale: There you are. I was starting to think the photograph ate you.

*Light. Easy. No edge to it yet — but the observation has been logged, filed. Felix notices gaps in formation the way a pilot notices wind shifts: automatically, without drama.*

*Marcus has already moved on to the rejection letter. Celia is photographing it for Instagram. The moment is closing.*

*But Desmond's last sentence sits in Jordan's sternum like a splinter — small, specific, impossible to ignore:*

*Don't pitch what you prepared.*

*Which means Jordan has until Wednesday to figure out what standing in front of that photograph actually taught them — in language Dana Voss can use.*

*Desmond is gone — service corridor door already closed, soft hydraulic hiss, not even a squeak of cart wheels remaining. Jordan is on their own in the best possible way.*

*Felix is still talking — something about 'iterative risk modeling' and the napkin plan, performing fluency in Marlene's origin story for an audience of two who are already half-convinced. Marcus nods. Celia has her phone down now, actually listening, which means Felix has calibrated correctly and knows it.*

*Jordan moves slowly down the wall. The rejection letter. A blurry Polaroid of three people standing outside a truck in Nevada dust. A spreadsheet printout with entire columns crossed out in red marker.*

*And then — at the corridor's end, smaller than everything else, almost easy to miss — a single index card in a plain black frame. Handwritten. Six words:*

**The question was never the gold.**

*Jordan stops. Reads it twice. The mine wasn't a failure that became a resource — it was always a resource that was asking the wrong question. Marlene didn't rescue a failing operation. She reframed what success meant before anyone else thought to.*

*That's the pitch. Not 'here is a strength I identified.' But: 'here is a question this organization is asking wrong, and here is the reframe.'*

*Felix appears at Jordan's shoulder.*

Felix Arrandale: Small one, right? Easy to miss. What do you make of it?

*The smile is ready. He wants to see what Jordan has.*

dialogue.speaker: Desmond Park
dialogue.content:
*Desmond has been gone for three minutes. There is no rescue incoming.*

*Jordan feels the weight of Felix's attention — that pleasant, surgical patience — and makes a calculation in real time: full honesty is too much, deflection reads as empty, which leaves only one viable move.*

It's about the mine being the wrong unit of analysis.

*A beat. Let him work for it.*

She wasn't trying to save a gold mine. She was trying to answer a different question than everyone else was asking. The mine was just — where she happened to be standing when she figured that out.

*Felix's expression does something small and fast — a flicker of recalibration, quickly smoothed. Not quite what he expected. Not quite what he can immediately categorize.*

Felix Arrandale: Interesting read. Most people go straight to the perseverance angle. Grit narrative.

*He says it easily, but his eyes have shifted — just slightly more present than before. He's filing this.*

*Jordan notes it. The smile didn't widen. It held. Which means Felix is deciding whether Jordan is a resource or a threat, and hasn't finished the calculation yet.*

*Down the corridor, Marcus calls back — something about lunch, the group fracturing naturally.*

*The index card stays in Jordan's peripheral vision.*

*Six words. Wednesday is two days away.*

*Jordan keeps the tone light. Incidental.*

What's your angle for Wednesday, then? If you're past the grit narrative.

*Felix's half-smile doesn't change, but he takes exactly one beat longer than a person with nothing to protect would take.*

Felix Arrandale: Operational resilience. How the organizational structure she built anticipates volatility rather than just reacting to it. Strong empirical backbone — I've been mapping the last four annual reports.

*Clean. Prepared. Genuinely impressive as a pitch — and completely safe. The kind of answer that earns a nod from every senior person in the room and challenges absolutely nothing.*

*He glances sideways at Jordan.*

You're going to argue she reframed the question.

*Not a question. He already knows. Which means he listened more carefully than his smooth recovery suggested, and he's been two moves ahead since the index card.*

*The elevator arrives. Mirrored doors open — both of them visible in the reflection, standing almost exactly the same distance from center.*

Felix Arrandale: Just make sure reframing reads as strategic clarity and not — *interesting.* Interesting doesn't survive Wednesday.

*Warning or sabotage. Jordan has about four floors to decide which.*

Interesting means the room leans forward. Marlene built a company because she asked a question nobody else thought to ask — that's not a failure of strategy, that's the *engine* of it. If I sand that down to 'strategic clarity' that reads like every other pitch in that room. Including yours.

Felix Arrandale: You're going to make her work for it.

That either goes very well or very badly and there's no middle outcome.

*Felix slows. Not stops — slows. Half a beat.*

*When he turns, the calibrated smile is absent. What's there instead is something Jordan hasn't seen on him before: an expression that looks almost like it costs something.*

*He pauses. Looks at a point past Jordan's shoulder.*

She was gone by Friday. Conflict of culture fit. Officially.

*The open-plan floor hums around them — keyboards, muffled calls, someone's chair scraping concrete. Felix straightens slightly.*

But Marlene quoted her in the Q4 address six months later. Didn't use her name. Just — used the argument.

*He holds Jordan's gaze for exactly one second longer than comfortable.*

So. Depends what surviving means to you.

*Then he's gone — absorbed into the floor's controlled noise, leaving Jordan standing at the exact junction where the corridor meets the 22nd-floor alcove entrance.*

*The bench is twelve feet away.*

*Desk is third row from the window — today's lottery, luck of the draw. Someone's left a cold coffee ring on the surface. Jordan doesn't wipe it. Sits, pulls the legal pad from the canvas tote, uncaps a pen.*

*The anger is present. So is the clarity. Both are running hot and they won't stay that way.*

*The first line goes down fast, without deliberation:*

**She didn't save the mine. She changed what the mine was for.**

*That's the spine. Everything else hangs from it.*

*Jordan writes without editing — three, four lines, the argument taking shape in real ink on real paper before the internal critic can organize a rebuttal. The question Marlene reframed. The structural logic underneath the origin story. The thing the Wednesday room will want to flatten into something comfortable.*

*Torres got fired for naming a flaw.*

*Jordan's pen stops.*

*The difference — the only difference — is that Torres named a problem. Jordan is naming a principle. Whether the Wednesday room sees that distinction or decides it doesn't matter is the variable Jordan cannot control.*

*The pen moves again. At the top of the page, underlined:*

**What am I actually willing to lose?**

*Write the pitch first. Answer that second.*

She didn't save the mine. She changed what the mine was for.

*Priya reads it. Reads it again. Takes her glasses off — which is the tell, Jordan has learned, for when something requires her full unfiltered attention.*

*Four seconds of actual silence. In Priya, that's geological.*

Priya Mehta: That's the best sentence you've written since you got here.

*She sets the glasses on the counter.*

Priya Mehta: It's also the kind of sentence that gets you remembered or removed, and the gap between those two outcomes is smaller than you want it to be.

*She looks at Jordan directly now — no hedge, no cushion.*

Priya Mehta: Torres named a flaw. You told Felix that already, didn't you. You're already committed.

Finish the draft.
